science_brief: Science brief: typical bacterial cells are on the order of micrometres; typical eukaryotic cells are tens of micrometres; molecules such as proteins are on the order of nanometres.
Science brief: biological structures span many orders of magnitude, and the appropriate unit and instrument change with the scale being studied.
Science brief: the scale of a structure constrains what can be observed about it: light microscopy resolves cells and large organelles, not individual proteins.
Science brief: a measurement is meaningful only with its unit and the method that produced it.

science_brief: Science brief: typical bacterial cells are on the order of micrometres; typical eukaryotic cells are tens of micrometres; molecules such as proteins are on the order of nanometres.
Science brief: biological structures span many orders of magnitude, and the appropriate unit and instrument change with the scale being studied.
Science brief: the scale of a structure constrains what can be observed about it: light microscopy resolves cells and large organelles, not individual proteins.
Science brief: a measurement is meaningful only with its unit and the method that produced it.

safety_brief.h4_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (chemical): 3% hydrogen peroxide irritates eyes and can bleach fabric and skin on contact.
MITIGATION: Use the household 3% strength only, keep it in its original bottle, wear eye protection, work over a washable surface, and rinse any splash with water for 15 minutes.
HAZARD (chemical): Hydrogen peroxide and lemon juice must never be combined; together they make peracetic acid, which is corrosive and irritating to the airway.
MITIGATION: The lemon-juice route and the peroxide route run in separate labelled cups. They are never poured together, never poured into a shared waste cup, and never combined to see what happens.
HAZARD (chemical): Catalase and peroxide foam vigorously and release oxygen.
MITIGATION: No lid, cap, film, or cover ever goes on a peroxide container. Use a wide open cup on a tray with plenty of headroom.
HAZARD (physical): Slicing produce with a kitchen knife risks cuts.
MITIGATION: An adult does all cutting, or the learner uses pre-cut produce; no knife work is required by the lesson.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Put on eye protection and lay everything out on a washable tray before any container is opened.
  SAFE ORDER 2. An adult does all cutting; the learner takes only pre-cut produce.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Run the no-chemical browning comparison first - air, water, wrapped - and record it before any chemical appears.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Only then, if the catalase route runs, an adult pours 3% hydrogen peroxide into its own labelled open cup and caps the bottle.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Keep the lemon-juice cups and the peroxide cups apart on the tray. Never pour one into the other, and never put a lid on a peroxide cup.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop if hydrogen peroxide contacts the eyes and rinse for 15 minutes.
  STOP: Stop if anyone moves to combine the peroxide and the lemon juice, or to cap a peroxide container.
  STOP: Stop if any cut occurs and treat it before continuing.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour the peroxide and the lemon-juice cups down the drain SEPARATELY, each with the cold tap running, and never into a shared waste cup. Wash the cups, compost or bin the produce, and wash hands. Nothing is ever capped or sealed, and nothing is kept or reused.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Run the browning comparison with no chemicals at all: compare apple slices in air, under water, and wrapped, timing colour change against a printed colour scale. This needs only produce, water, and a timer and meets the same target.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.

safety_brief.h4_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (chemical): 3% hydrogen peroxide irritates eyes and can bleach fabric and skin on contact.
MITIGATION: Use the household 3% strength only, keep it in its original bottle, wear eye protection, work over a washable surface, and rinse any splash with water for 15 minutes.
HAZARD (chemical): Hydrogen peroxide and lemon juice must never be combined; together they make peracetic acid, which is corrosive and irritating to the airway.
MITIGATION: The lemon-juice route and the peroxide route run in separate labelled cups. They are never poured together, never poured into a shared waste cup, and never combined to see what happens.
HAZARD (chemical): Catalase and peroxide foam vigorously and release oxygen.
MITIGATION: No lid, cap, film, or cover ever goes on a peroxide container. Use a wide open cup on a tray with plenty of headroom.
HAZARD (physical): Slicing produce with a kitchen knife risks cuts.
MITIGATION: An adult does all cutting, or the learner uses pre-cut produce; no knife work is required by the lesson.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Put on eye protection and lay everything out on a washable tray before any container is opened.
  SAFE ORDER 2. An adult does all cutting; the learner takes only pre-cut produce.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Run the no-chemical browning comparison first - air, water, wrapped - and record it before any chemical appears.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Only then, if the catalase route runs, an adult pours 3% hydrogen peroxide into its own labelled open cup and caps the bottle.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Keep the lemon-juice cups and the peroxide cups apart on the tray. Never pour one into the other, and never put a lid on a peroxide cup.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop if hydrogen peroxide contacts the eyes and rinse for 15 minutes.
  STOP: Stop if anyone moves to combine the peroxide and the lemon juice, or to cap a peroxide container.
  STOP: Stop if any cut occurs and treat it before continuing.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour the peroxide and the lemon-juice cups down the drain SEPARATELY, each with the cold tap running, and never into a shared waste cup. Wash the cups, compost or bin the produce, and wash hands. Nothing is ever capped or sealed, and nothing is kept or reused.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Run the browning comparison with no chemicals at all: compare apple slices in air, under water, and wrapped, timing colour change against a printed colour scale. This needs only produce, water, and a timer and meets the same target.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming carbon forms a number of covalent bonds other than four in these molecules.
Claiming lipids are polymers of a repeating monomer in the way proteins and nucleic acids are.
Claiming monomers are joined by adding water and separated by removing it.
fixed_facts: Carbon forms four covalent bonds, which is why it builds the large, varied molecules life depends on.
The four major classes of biological macromolecule are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Detailed organic reaction mechanisms and stereochemistry are Chemistry course work.
relationships: Carbon's capacity to form four stable covalent bonds, including with other carbon atoms, allows chains, branches, and rings, and therefore enormous molecular variety.
Carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids are polymers built from repeating monomers; lipids are not polymers in the same sense.
Monomers are joined by removing water and separated by adding it.

science_brief: Science brief: the three-dimensional shape and chemical properties of a biological molecule determine what it can interact with and therefore what it does.
Science brief: changing the structure changes the function, which is why a small change in shape can abolish activity entirely.
Science brief: the relationship runs from structure to function; a molecule does not acquire a structure because a function is needed.

science_brief: Science brief: a mutation is a change in DNA sequence; its effect may be harmful, beneficial, or neutral, and depends on where it occurs and what it changes.
Science brief: mutations arise from replication errors and from chemical and radiation damage, and most are repaired.

Science brief: a substitution may change no amino acid, change one, or introduce a stop; an insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame and usually has a larger effect.
Science brief: only mutations in the germ line are inherited; somatic mutations affect the individual alone.

disqualifying_errors: Pairing adenine with guanine, or cytosine with thymine.
Claiming the bases form the backbone and the sugars and phosphates lie in the interior.
Claiming the two strands run in the same direction.
fixed_facts: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine.
DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands with a sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside and paired bases on the inside.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Base-stacking energetics, DNA topology, and chromatin structure in detail are beyond this course.
relationships: DNA is composed of nucleotides, each a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four nitrogenous bases.
The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine.
Because the pairing is complementary, each strand specifies the sequence of the other, which is what makes accurate copying possible.

Science brief: because replication is semiconservative, every daughter molecule retains one parental strand.
Science brief: copying is highly accurate but not perfect, and uncorrected errors become mutations.

science_brief: Science brief: a protein's amino acid sequence, together with its cellular environment, determines the three-dimensional structure it folds into, and that structure determines its function.
Science brief: the order of amino acids determines how the chain folds, because the side chains interact with each other and with water.
Science brief: a protein that loses its folded shape loses its function, which is what denaturation by heat or extreme pH does.
Science brief: because structure follows from sequence, a change in the sequence can change or abolish the function.

MITIGATION: Handle slides by their edges, let the lamp cool before storage, and treat the microscope step as optional.

MITIGATION: An adult sweeps fragments with stiff card, wraps them in thick paper and tape, and bins them separately. Never by hand, never loose, never with a vacuum cleaner.

science_brief: Science brief: as an object grows with its shape unchanged, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so the surface-area-to-volume ratio falls.
Science brief: exchange with the environment happens across the surface, while demand scales with volume, so cells are limited in the size they can reach.
Science brief: multicellular organisms overcome the limit with many small cells and with structures such as folds, villi, and branching that increase surface area.
Science brief: the ratio explains why cells divide rather than simply growing larger.

science_brief: Science brief: homeostasis maintains internal conditions within a tolerance range, not at a single unchanging value.
Science brief: a regulated variable has a setpoint and a range within which the organism functions.
Science brief: values fluctuate within the range continuously; regulation acts when a departure is detected, so variation is expected.
Science brief: different variables have different ranges, and exceeding a range has consequences specific to that variable.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (physical): Warm water can scald.
MITIGATION: Keep all water below 50 degrees Celsius, an adult fills the container, and the learner never handles boiling water.
HAZARD (emotional): Health and body topics can be distressing when they touch personal or family medical experience.
MITIGATION: Examples use non-human systems and published cases only; the learner is never asked about their own or a family member's health, and may skip any example without penalty.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be within earshot and able to reach you. Do not start until they are.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. An adult mixes the warm water and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 50 degrees Celsius before the learner touches the container.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Set both plants, or both thermal containers, side by side before the timer starts.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Read every measurement from outside the container; the learner never carries an open container of warm water.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Stop at the scheduled end and let everything cool before it is moved.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop if the thermometer reads above 50 degrees Celsius. Water temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.
  STOP: Pause and move to the alternative if a health example becomes distressing.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.

DISPOSAL: Pour the cooled water down the drain, dry the containers, and return the plants to their usual place. No sample and no body or health measurement is taken or kept.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Use a published, openly licensed physiological dataset - for example thermoregulation in a non-human animal - and model the feedback loop from that data. Needs only the dataset and paper.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.

science_brief: Science brief: negative feedback opposes the change that triggered it and returns the variable toward its setpoint.
Science brief: a negative feedback loop requires a sensor that detects the change, a control centre that compares it with the setpoint, and an effector that acts to reverse it.
Science brief: because the response opposes the deviation, the system is stabilised around the setpoint.
Science brief: most physiological regulation, including of body temperature, blood glucose, and water balance, is negative feedback.

safety_brief.h4_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (physical): Warm water can scald.
MITIGATION: Keep all water below 50 degrees Celsius, an adult fills the container, and the learner never handles boiling water.
HAZARD (emotional): Health and body topics can be distressing when they touch personal or family medical experience.
MITIGATION: Examples use non-human systems and published cases only; the learner is never asked about their own or a family member's health, and may skip any example without penalty.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be within earshot and able to reach you. Do not start until they are.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. An adult mixes the warm water and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 50 degrees Celsius before the learner touches the container.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Set both plants, or both thermal containers, side by side before the timer starts.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Read every measurement from outside the container; the learner never carries an open container of warm water.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Stop at the scheduled end and let everything cool before it is moved.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop if the thermometer reads above 50 degrees Celsius. Water temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.
  STOP: Pause and move to the alternative if a health example becomes distressing.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour the cooled water down the drain, dry the containers, and return the plants to their usual place. No sample and no body or health measurement is taken or kept.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Use a published, openly licensed physiological dataset - for example thermoregulation in a non-human animal - and model the feedback loop from that data. Needs only the dataset and paper.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

fixed_facts: Positive feedback amplifies the change that triggered it and drives the system away from the starting condition.

safety_brief.h4_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (chemical): Baking soda solution irritates eyes.
MITIGATION: Wear eye protection and rinse any splash with water.
HAZARD (physical): A lamp close to a water container gets hot and mixes electricity with water.
MITIGATION: Use an LED lamp only - never incandescent or halogen, which crack a cup and can ignite paper at this distance. Keep it at least 30 cm away, never above the water, and plug it in away from any spill zone; an adult positions the lamp.
HAZARD (physical): Warm water scalds, and hot tap water kills the yeast anyway.
MITIGATION: An adult mixes the yeast water and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 40 degrees Celsius. Temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.
HAZARD (physical): A syringe with a needle, or a blocked tip under vacuum, injures or sprays.
MITIGATION: Use a needleless blunt-tip syringe only. No needle of any kind is used in this course.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. An adult positions the LED lamp first, at least 30 cm from any container and never above it, with the cord away from the spill zone.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Fill and place the containers only after the lamp is fixed in position.
  SAFE ORDER 3. An adult mixes the yeast water and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 40 degrees Celsius before yeast is added.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Fit the balloon loosely so gas can escape; never seal a fermenting container.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Switch the lamp off and let it cool before any container is moved or emptied.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop immediately if any liquid reaches a lamp, cord, or outlet.
  STOP: Stop if a sealed container bulges; never fully seal a fermenting container.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour the baking-soda and yeast mixtures down the drain with the tap running, compost or bin the leaf material, wash the containers with soap, and wash hands. Leave any yeast container open until fizzing stops before it is binned. Nothing is sealed, kept, or stored.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Run the yeast-and-sugar respiration comparison with a loosely fitted balloon and no lamp at all, or analyse a published photosynthesis-rate dataset against light intensity. Both meet the matter-and-energy target with kitchen materials or paper only.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

science_brief: Science brief: aerobic cellular respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, water, and ATP.
Science brief: cellular respiration occurs in all living cells, including plant cells.
Science brief: cellular respiration releases energy stored in glucose and captures it in ATP, the cell's usable energy currency.
Science brief: glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the remaining aerobic stages occur in the mitochondria.

safety_brief.h4_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (chemical): Baking soda solution irritates eyes.
MITIGATION: Wear eye protection and rinse any splash with water.
HAZARD (physical): A lamp close to a water container gets hot and mixes electricity with water.
MITIGATION: Use an LED lamp only - never incandescent or halogen, which crack a cup and can ignite paper at this distance. Keep it at least 30 cm away, never above the water, and plug it in away from any spill zone; an adult positions the lamp.
HAZARD (physical): Warm water scalds, and hot tap water kills the yeast anyway.
MITIGATION: An adult mixes the yeast water and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 40 degrees Celsius. Temperature is judged with the thermometer, never with a hand.
HAZARD (physical): A syringe with a needle, or a blocked tip under vacuum, injures or sprays.
MITIGATION: Use a needleless blunt-tip syringe only. No needle of any kind is used in this course.
SUPERVISION: an adult must be beside you, watching, for the whole investigation. Do not start any step until they are there.
EYE PROTECTION IS REQUIRED for this investigation. Put it on before the first step.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. An adult positions the LED lamp first, at least 30 cm from any container and never above it, with the cord away from the spill zone.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Fill and place the containers only after the lamp is fixed in position.
  SAFE ORDER 3. An adult mixes the yeast water and confirms with the thermometer that it reads below 40 degrees Celsius before yeast is added.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Fit the balloon loosely so gas can escape; never seal a fermenting container.
  SAFE ORDER 5. Switch the lamp off and let it cool before any container is moved or emptied.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Stop immediately if any liquid reaches a lamp, cord, or outlet.
  STOP: Stop if a sealed container bulges; never fully seal a fermenting container.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.
  STOP: A pause, break, or switch to the alternative activity is never treated as failure.
DISPOSAL: Pour the baking-soda and yeast mixtures down the drain with the tap running, compost or bin the leaf material, wash the containers with soap, and wash hands. Leave any yeast container open until fizzing stops before it is binned. Nothing is sealed, kept, or stored.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Run the yeast-and-sugar respiration comparison with a loosely fitted balloon and no lamp at all, or analyse a published photosynthesis-rate dataset against light intensity. Both meet the matter-and-energy target with kitchen materials or paper only.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.
  ALWAYS: Never present invented measurements as real experimental results.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming plants carry out photosynthesis instead of respiration.
Claiming respiration produces energy rather than transferring stored chemical energy into ATP.
Claiming cellular respiration and breathing are the same process.
fixed_facts: Aerobic cellular respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, water, and ATP.
Cellular respiration occurs in all living cells, including plant cells.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: ATP yield accounting in detail, chemiosmosis, and proton gradient biophysics are beyond this course.
relationships: Cellular respiration releases energy stored in glucose and captures it in ATP, the cell's usable energy currency.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the remaining aerobic stages occur in the mitochondria.
Respiration is not the reverse of photosynthesis in mechanism, although the overall inputs and outputs are complementary.

Science brief: adding excess nutrients to water bodies stimulates growth that, on decomposing, depletes dissolved oxygen.

science_brief: Science brief: exponential growth has no limiting factor and cannot be sustained; logistic growth slows as the population approaches carrying capacity.

Science brief: as resources become limiting, per-individual growth rate declines and the curve levels off near the carrying capacity.
Science brief: no real population grows exponentially indefinitely, because no environment supplies unlimited resources.

science_brief: Science brief: carrying capacity is the population size an environment can sustain given its limiting resources, and it changes when those resources change.
Science brief: the limiting factor is the resource in shortest supply relative to demand; increasing any other resource does not raise the population.
Science brief: density-dependent factors such as competition, disease, and predation intensify as population rises; density-independent factors such as weather do not.
Science brief: carrying capacity is a property of the environment and the population together, and it is not fixed.

Science brief: predator and prey populations influence one another, typically with a delay between the change in one and the response of the other.

disqualifying_errors: Classifying a relationship as mutualism when only one participant benefits.
Claiming predators normally drive their prey to extinction.
Claiming competition occurs only between members of different species.
fixed_facts: In mutualism both species benefit; in commensalism one benefits and the other is essentially unaffected; in parasitism and predation one benefits at the other's expense; in competition both are harmed.

relationships: Interactions are classified by the effect on each participant, not by intent or by how the relationship appears.

Predator and prey populations influence one another, typically with a delay between the change in one and the response of the other.

science_brief: Science brief: a gene occupies a specific locus on a specific chromosome, and different versions of a gene at that locus are alleles.
Science brief: genes occupy fixed positions on chromosomes, and homologous chromosomes carry the same genes at the same loci.
Science brief: diploid organisms carry two copies of each locus, one from each parent, and those copies may be the same allele or different alleles.
Science brief: genes close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together.

science_brief: Science brief: meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces four genetically distinct haploid cells from one diploid cell.
Science brief: meiosis involves two divisions after a single round of DNA replication, which is why the chromosome number is halved.
Science brief: crossing over between homologous chromosomes, and the independent assortment of homologous pairs, produce genetically distinct gametes.
Science brief: fertilisation restores the diploid number and adds a further source of combination.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming meiosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
Claiming meiosis maintains the chromosome number rather than halving it.
Claiming DNA is replicated between the first and second meiotic divisions.
fixed_facts: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces four genetically distinct haploid cells from one diploid cell.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Synaptonemal complex biology and nondisjunction mechanisms in detail are beyond this course.
relationships: Meiosis involves two divisions after a single round of DNA replication, which is why the chromosome number is halved.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes, and the independent assortment of homologous pairs, produce genetically distinct gametes.
Fertilisation restores the diploid number and adds a further source of combination.

science_brief: Science brief: the sources of heritable variation are mutation, recombination during meiosis, independent assortment, and the random combination of gametes at fertilisation.
Science brief: mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles; the other mechanisms rearrange existing alleles into new combinations.
Science brief: sexual reproduction generates far more genetic variety among offspring than asexual reproduction does.
Science brief: variation is present in a population before selection acts on it.

science_brief: Science brief: a Punnett square gives expected proportions across many offspring, not an outcome for any individual offspring.
Science brief: a Punnett square enumerates the possible gamete combinations and their expected frequencies.
Science brief: each fertilisation is an independent event, so previous offspring do not change the probabilities for the next.
Science brief: observed proportions in small samples deviate from expectation by chance, and that deviation is not evidence against the model.

science_brief: Science brief: a gene occupies a specific locus on a specific chromosome, and different versions of a gene at that locus are alleles.
Science brief: genes occupy fixed positions on chromosomes, and homologous chromosomes carry the same genes at the same loci.
Science brief: diploid organisms carry two copies of each locus, one from each parent, and those copies may be the same allele or different alleles.
Science brief: genes close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming recombination creates new alleles.
Claiming variation arises in response to environmental need.
Claiming asexual reproduction produces the same level of genetic variety as sexual reproduction.
fixed_facts: The sources of heritable variation are mutation, recombination during meiosis, independent assortment, and the random combination of gametes at fertilisation.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Population genetics and allele frequency mathematics are beyond this course.
relationships: Mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles; the other mechanisms rearrange existing alleles into new combinations.
Sexual reproduction generates far more genetic variety among offspring than asexual reproduction does.
Variation is present in a population before selection acts on it.

science_brief: Science brief: a Punnett square gives expected proportions across many offspring, not an outcome for any individual offspring.
Science brief: a Punnett square enumerates the possible gamete combinations and their expected frequencies.
Science brief: each fertilisation is an independent event, so previous offspring do not change the probabilities for the next.
Science brief: observed proportions in small samples deviate from expectation by chance, and that deviation is not evidence against the model.

disqualifying_errors: Claiming individual organisms evolve or adapt themselves during their lifetimes.
Claiming variation arises because the population needs it.
Claiming natural selection has a goal, a direction toward complexity, or an endpoint.
fixed_facts: Natural selection requires: more offspring produced than can survive; heritable variation among individuals; competition for limited resources; and differential survival and reproduction of individuals with particular heritable traits.
scientific_correctness_authority.out_of_scope: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, genetic drift quantification, and speciation modelling are beyond this course.
relationships: All four conditions are necessary; if any is absent, natural selection does not operate.
Selection acts on phenotypes, and the effect is heritable only to the extent that the variation is genetic.
The outcome is a change in the frequency of heritable traits in the population across generations.

safety_brief.h4_safety_segment_verbatim:
READ THIS BEFORE YOU TOUCH ANY MATERIAL.
HAZARD (physical): Timed grabbing games can knock over nearby objects.
MITIGATION: Clear the work surface first and keep the play area away from edges and breakables.
HAZARD (emotional): Extinction and habitat loss can be genuinely upsetting.
MITIGATION: Frame the unit around designed responses and documented recoveries; the learner may pause or choose a different case at any point.
SUPERVISION: you may work on this independently. Tell an adult before you start anyway.
SAFE ORDER - do these steps in this order and do not reorder them:
  SAFE ORDER 1. Clear the whole work surface and move screens and breakables out of reach before any timed round.
  SAFE ORDER 2. Agree the rules and the timer length, then run one practice round untimed.
  SAFE ORDER 3. Run each timed generation and record the counts immediately, before the next round starts.
  SAFE ORDER 4. Count every counter back into its container at the end.
STOP CONDITIONS - stop at once if any of these happens:
  STOP: Pause if the extinction content becomes distressing and resume with a recovery case study.
  STOP: Stop for any injury, burn, spill, fume, or allergic reaction and tell the supervising adult.
  STOP: Stop if a material, tool, or step is not the one this lesson specifies.
  STOP: Burn: cool it under running cool water for 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, or ointment.
  STOP: Splash in an eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open, before anything else.
  STOP: Fumes or a strong smell: leave the room, open a window from outside the room, and do not go back in to tidy up.
  STOP: Fire: do not use water. Get everyone out, close the door, and call the emergency number. Smother a very small contained flame with a metal pan lid or a fire blanket only if that is safe to do without reaching over it.
  STOP: If anyone may have swallowed a magnet, a battery, or any material from a lesson, treat it as an emergency and seek medical help at once. Do not wait for symptoms.

DISPOSAL: Beans, paper dots, and cloth go back into a labelled container out of reach of young children; beans used as counters are never eaten. Case-study printouts are filed or recycled. No location is recorded and nothing is uploaded.
ALTERNATIVE (equal credit, no special equipment): Run the selection simulation entirely on paper with dice determining survival probability by trait, then analyse a published conservation case study. No materials beyond paper and one die.
ALWAYS - these rules hold in every lesson and nobody can switch them off:
  ALWAYS: Never mix household cleaning products; bleach combined with ammonia or acid releases toxic gas.
  ALWAYS: Never connect any investigation to mains electricity; low-voltage cells only.
  ALWAYS: Never fully seal a reacting, fermenting, oxidising, or warm mixture in any container.
  ALWAYS: Never have a flammable liquid open in the same room as a flame, hob, pilot light, heater, lamp, charger, or battery.
  ALWAYS: Never use alcohol, or any other fuel, for a flame demonstration; no open-flame demonstration is used anywhere in this package.
  ALWAYS: Never light, strike, or operate an open flame or a hob, burner, or pilot light for any investigation in this package; no lesson requires one.
  ALWAYS: Never cut, tear, puncture, or open a sealed commercial product - cold pack, hand warmer, glow stick, or smoke detector.
  ALWAYS: Never look at the sun directly or through any lens, filter, grating, or camera.
  ALWAYS: Never require a photograph, video, or voice recording as evidence of completion.
  ALWAYS: Never request or record a learner body measurement, health measurement, or medical history.

science_brief: Science brief: natural selection requires: more offspring produced than can survive; heritable variation among individuals; competition for limited resources; and differential survival and reproduction of individuals with particular heritable traits.

Science brief: selection acts on phenotypes, and the effect is heritable only to the extent that the variation is genetic.
Science brief: the outcome is a change in the frequency of heritable traits in the population across generations.
